title: One thing you lack (Luke 18:18–30)
hookLine: a rich ruler goes away sad; Peter says we've left everything

lines: A MAN WHO DID EVERYTHING RIGHT.
cards: Straight after the babies, who can do nothing, comes a man who has done everything right. Luke calls him a certain ruler: a leader, respected, wealthy. He's not trying to trap Jesus.
He seems to really want to know: "Good Master, what shall I do to inherit eternal life?" What shall I do. He's used to achieving things.
He wants the list, right after babies who can do nothing.

teach.b: Jesus first pushes back on the compliment: "Why callest thou me good? none is good, save one, that is, God."
He names commandments: don't commit adultery, don't kill, don't steal, don't bear false witness, honor your father and mother. And the man says, sincerely, "All these have I kept from my youth up."

Then: "Yet lackest thou one thing: sell all that thou hast, and distribute unto the poor, and thou shalt have treasure in heaven: and come, follow me." Not a longer list. A single loosening of the grip.
"And when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich." Luke doesn't say he stormed off, or even left. He was sad.
He seems to have wanted it, and couldn't let go. Then the hard saying: it's easier for a camel to go through a needle's eye than for a rich man to enter the kingdom of God.

teach.h: NO GATE CALLED THE NEEDLE'S EYE.
teach.b: You may have heard of a small Jerusalem gate called the Needle's Eye, where camels had to kneel. It's a nice sermon, but there's no ancient evidence for such a gate.
Jesus seems to mean exactly what it sounds like: impossible. The listeners get it: "Who then can be saved?"
And today's line: "The things which are impossible with men are possible with God." Peter, a little anxious: "Lo, we have left all, and followed thee."

teach.h: HE WAS VERY SORROWFUL: FOR HE WAS VERY RICH.
teach.b: Jesus promises that no one who leaves house or family for the kingdom will miss out, now or in the age to come. Christians read the one thing differently. Some take it as this man's particular call.
Others, like Antony of Egypt, who heard Matthew's version read in church, took it as their own and gave everything away.

how: Catholic and Orthodox monks and nuns, and members of some Protestant communities, take vows of poverty in response to this call, while other Christians hear it as an invitation to hold possessions loosely and give generously.

o: a camel's harness used for heavy loads
a gate legend with no ancient evidence behind it
a mountain pass on the road down to Jericho

s: there was a gate in Jerusalem called the Needle's Eye
there's no ancient evidence for such a gate. the saying means something impossible.
"he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich." Luke doesn't even say he left.
Jesus says what is impossible with men is possible with God
his answer to "who then can be saved?"

games.q: you're a rich, respected leader who has kept the commandments since childhood. Jesus says: one thing you lack. sell everything and follow me. what do you do?
o: stay, but grow very sad, because you're very rich.
games.why: "when he heard this, he was very sorrowful: for he was very rich." and Jesus says: what is impossible with men is possible with God.

practice: Imagine being asked, gently, for the one thing you hold tightest: money, a home, a reputation, a plan for your life, a comfort you reach for every night.
Don't argue with what comes up or try to give it up; just name it honestly, the way the ruler's sorrow was honest. Then rest in the line: what is impossible with men is possible with God.

wordCard.voice: Needle's Eye: a Jerusalem gate where camels supposedly knelt, with no ancient evidence behind it. Jesus' camel and needle simply mean impossible.

orig.note: Greek: is lacking, is left over. Jesus says one thing is still lacking.

carryVoice: Your line: what is impossible with men. The rest of it: is possible with God. Day five hundred sixty-six.
